Track 1: Energy
BNEF Talk: Critical Minerals – Where Are the Bottlenecks to a Breakthrough?
items.synopsisMd: Growing demand for critical minerals driven by the energy transition has put the mining sector in the spotlight. Governments want to build resilient supply chains, companies want secure access to supply and investors want greater exposure to the sector. Yet significant bottlenecks remain. Early stage projects struggle to access financing, major projects face regulatory delays and supply-chain emissions continue to rise. This talk will explore how the industry can address these challenges while capturing the opportunities they create.

items.name: Europe’s Industrial Transition: A Test of Competitiveness
items.synopsisMd: Europe’s industrial transition is at a critical juncture. Governments want to cut emissions while protecting competitiveness, jobs and energy security, but the pathways are increasingly difficult to finance and deliver. Electrification depends on affordable power and grid access, while carbon capture and storage (CCS) and hydrogen clusters need long-term policy support, credible demand and bankable risk allocation. The UK’s clean industrial clusters offer a test case for Europe. Can this model revive industry and provide a template for decarbonization, or is it reaching its limits? Can Europe enable more clean industry projects to take final investment decisions, without pushing production offshore?

items.name: Networking Reception
Who Builds, Pays for and Profits From the Grid?
items.synopsisMd: Europe is entering a decisive phase in grid development, where speed is critical but the current market-led model risks continually falling behind as networks take longer to build than clean power capacity or industrial projects. The UK’s Clean Power 2030 plan points toward a more coordinated approach, raising a central question: who should take control of the next phase of grid expansion? Should governments direct investment, should network operators be empowered to build ahead of demand, or can markets and private finance still deliver at the pace required? Central to these questions is a fundamental challenge: can Europe make rational investment decisions while continuing to treat the grid as a cost to be minimized rather than as critical economic infrastructure? Ultimately, however, none of this will matter if permitting constraints continue to determine when – or even if – the grid gets built.

items.name: BNEF Talk: The Transition Trap – Cutting Supply Before Demand Is Ready
items.synopsisMd: Europe’s energy crisis showed the risks of reducing or disrupting fossil fuel supply before demand has been structurally reduced: price spikes volatility and wider economic impacts. This talk will examine why the energy transition is more resilient when clean technologies reduce fossil-fuel demand, rather than when supply is abruptly constrained.

items.synopsisMd: A UK-focused fireside chat on what it will take to accelerate Europe’s nuclear revival, from reducing regulatory barriers and unlocking new financing models to advancing small modular reactions (SMRs) and applying lessons from major nuclear projects.

items.name: Adapt or Mitigate? Investment Growth in the Transition's Next Decade
items.synopsisMd: Banks, asset managers, insurers and infrastructure owners are making bets across mitigation, adaptation and resilience activities. But physical climate damage, saturation in mature climate technologies, and energy security risks are shifting where investment opportunities lie, from long-term mitigation to asset-level resilience. Where will capital see the highest return in the next decade? How are financial institutions evaluating, and venturing into, decarbonization and adaptation opportunities?

items.name: Electricity Reliability: New Revenue Models to Ensure Security of Supply
items.synopsisMd: Clean power increasingly needs to be firm, not just cheap. As renewables grow, coal retires and large electricity consumers such as data centers and industrial clusters seek reliable supply, Europe must decide what will provide dependable capacity in a cleaner grid. This session will examine which technologies are emerging as viable solutions – from batteries, long-duration storage and pumped hydro to demand flexibility, gas peakers, nuclear and other clean dispatchable options – and what it will take to make them bankable. Which policy instruments and structures are best placed to finance firm capacity going forward? And how can reliability be secured without locking in unnecessary cost, emissions or stranded assets?

items.name: Corporate Energy Procurement: Bridging the Clean Power Price Gap
items.synopsisMd: Corporate power buyers want clean electricity, price protection and credible decarbonization claims, but European power markets are becoming harder to contract amid rising policy uncertainty. Negative prices, volume risk, policy uncertainty and the cost of firming intermittent supply are widening the gap between what buyers are wiling to pay and what developers need to finance projects. Where is the bid-ask spread most visible, and what are buyers, sellers and lenders prioritizing in negotiations? Are buyers willing to pay enough for shaped, firmed or 24/7 clean-power products to support project economics? Can corporate procurement still drive additional renewables buildout in a more volatile and policy-sensitive power market?

items.name: The Future of Flexibility: Business Models and Opportunities for Grids Operators
items.synopsisMd: Europe’s next grid constraint will be on our doorsteps. Electric vehicles, heat pumps, rooftop solar and residential batteries are placing increasing pressure on local distribution networks, while also creating opportunities for every home to become active participants in the power system. Can local flexibility reduce the need for costly grid reinforcement, or merely delay it? Who will control and benefit from local flexibility – retailers, aggregators or distribution system operators? And as local networks become more active, should Europe rely on market signals such as local pricing, or give grid operators a stronger role in planning and dispatching flexibility?

items.name: Made in Europe, Heated by Europe
items.subtitle: Themed lunch hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd: Heat pump adoption in Europe is back in focus as geopolitical shocks are reshaping the case for heat pumps, both in homes and industrial process heat. Unlike solar and batteries, heat pumps are a genuine Made-in-Europe success story, yet policy reversals and price sensitivity have kept the market fragile and investors cautious. Can Europe turn a second energy security crisis into a durable heat pump supercycle, and is now the moment to scale capital into European heat pump manufacturing and deployment? What policy architecture is needed to make heat pumps the backbone of Europe’s competitive, decarbonized building stock? And could a Europe-wide clean heat market mechanism, modelled on the UK’s scheme, materially accelerate market growth?

items.name: BNEF Talk: When Weather Moves Europe’s Energy Markets
items.synopsisMd: Weather is becoming one of the most important forces shaping Europe’s energy system, shaping power demand, renewable generation, gas consumption, storage dynamics and cross-border market dynamics. This talk will explore how changing weather patterns are affecting European energy markets, where weather-related chokepoints are emerging across power, gas and energy transition infrastructure, and how improved forecasting can provide greater visibility into high-impact events and support better operational and investment decisions.

items.name: Inside the AI Data Center: What Are the Cutting Edge Technologies and What Impact Will They Have?
items.synopsisMd: AI is reshaping data center technology far beyond chip design. The race to build gigascale AI infrastructure is driving rapid innovation in how power is delivered to processors, how chips are cooled, how information moves at high speed, and how data centers interact with the grid. Data centers have become incubators for next-generation technologies, from direct-current power architectures and advanced liquid cooling to fiber optics and energy storage. This session will explore the technologies enabling the next wave of AI innovation, and what it means for the broader energy and power electronics sectors.

Assessing Banks’ Transition: Investor Expectations Amid New Realities and Competing Metrics
items.subtitle: Themed lunch hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd: Banks are increasingly positioning their role in the transition as enabling real-economy decarbonization, emphasizing the corporate action, policy support and technology progress required to deploy capital effectively. At the same time, they are being asked to support fossil fuel clients facing market volatility, engage with hard-to-abate sectors that may increase financed emissions and demonstrate credible transition strategies as policy, technology and market realities reshape the pace of climate action. This session will examine how asset owners and asset managers are reassessing banks’ climate progress, which signals matter most, where current metrics may fall short and what additional disclosures investors need to hold banks accountable.

items.name: Can Europe Turn Natural Gas Volatility Into Clean Power Momentum?
items.synopsisMd: High gas prices can strengthen the case for electrification, but they can also raise electricity prices, erode industrial competitiveness, weaken demand and test public support for the transition. As Europe reduces its reliance on gas, the fuel’s role in the power system is also evolving from a source of baseload generation and a key price-setting technology toward a provider of flexibility, backup capacity and security of supply. How should Europe manage gas volatility while accelerating clean power deployment? Can higher gas prices drive decarbonization, or do they risk slowing demand and investment? What role should gas-fired generation, liquefied natural gas, storage, batteries, demand response and capacity markets play in maintaining a reliable and affordable power system?

The Energy Transition Dividend: Can Emerging Markets Turn Decarbonization Into Growth, Investment and Competitiveness?
items.subtitle: Themed lunch hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd: As world leaders prepare for COP31, emerging markets are increasingly focused on a broader question: how can the transition drive economic growth, strengthen competitiveness and attract investment? This session will explore what separates the leaders from the laggards and how the next phase of the transition is being shaped by economics, geopolitics and industrial strategy.

items.name: Summit Welcome
How Storage and Renewables Are Rewriting Power Asset Returns
items.synopsisMd: The business case for renewable energy is changing rapidly. Energy storage and wind additions are rising in Europe, while stand-alone solar additions may have peaked in 2025. As wholesale price volatility reshapes project economics, developers and investors are rethinking how clean power assets are contracted, financed and operated. Co-location, offtake agreements, hedging and active asset management are increasingly important in protecting returns and creating asset value. At the same time, power market designs are changing as governments seek to balance affordability, resilience and economic security. This panel will explore where the returns are emerging across renewables and energy storage. Which near-term risks are real, and which are noise? How are developers and investors underwriting solar, wind and storage in a more volatile market? And who is best positioned to capture value in the next phase of Europe’s clean-power buildout?

items.name: Reshaping Europe’s Strategic Future
items.synopsisMd: The Ukraine war, the Iran conflict, and trade tensions have forced Europe through a series of hard lessons. They have exposed the real costs of dependence on foreign trading partners, vulnerability to volatile fossil fuel markets, and unresolved tensions between energy security and climate ambitions. These pressures are reshaping corporate strategy, supply-chain viability, competitiveness and investment priorities across the region. What has Europe learned from navigating these pressures? Where has it responded effectively and where has it fallen short? And where do credible opportunities exist in the energy transition and resilience-building as geopolitical uncertainty becomes a more permanent feature of the landscape?

items.name: BNEF Talk: Energy Shocks and the New Corporate Transition Risk
items.synopsisMd: Geopolitical conflict and volatile oil and gas prices can quickly reshape the economics of the energy transition. This talk will examine, through both macroeconomic and company-level perspectives, how an energy shock affects demand, margins, carbon exposure and capital spending across key sectors. Which companies benefit from higher prices, which face rising transition risk, and which risks arrive sooner than expected?

items.name: BNEF Talk: From a Solar Boom to a Race for Clean Firm Capacity
items.synopsisMd: Solar is transforming power markets, but its success is creating challenges for asset owners and the power system. Negative prices, lower capture rates and revenue uncertainty are accelerating the shift toward storage, co-location and portfolio strategies. BloombergNEF expects nearly 30% of new global solar projects to be paired with energy storage this year. At the same time, growth in data centers, rising industrial demand and energy security concerns are raising demand for power that is both clean and dependable. This talk will examine how much clean firm capacity solar and storage can provide – and where complementary technologies such as wind, nuclear, gas and long-duration energy storage may be needed to close the gap.

Markets on the Rise: Which New Countries Deliver Storage and Clean Power Returns?
items.synopsisMd: Mature European power markets are becoming more crowded, increasingly affected by price cannibalization and harder to underwrite. But rising power demand, growing storage needs and improving clean-energy economics are creating new opportunities for European developers, investors and banks across Southern and Eastern Europe. The session will open with a BNEF perspective on investment trends and market fundamentals, including insights from the upcoming Central and Southeast Europe Energy Market Outlook, before moving to a panel discussion on where capital can find growth, which risks matter most, and which markets are investable today rather than simply promising.

items.name: Future of Profitability in Commercial Vehicle Fleet Electrification
items.subtitle: Themed lunch hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd: The economics of battery-electric vans and trucks become increasingly competitive across parts of Europe’s commercial fleet market, particularly in urban delivery, regional logistics and return-to-base operations. Rising fuel costs are also putting pressure on fleet operators’ margins, strengthening the case for electrification as a way to reduce exposure to volatile energy prices. Yet broader adoption remains constrained by high upfront costs, uncertain residual values, uneven access to charging infrastructure, and the complexity of deploying infrastructure across fragmented markets. This session will explore how fleet electrification and infrastructure can scale, and the business models, and financing structures needed to unlock long-term investment in Europe’s commercial fleet transition.

items.name: Opening BNEF Talk by BNEF CEO
Clean Fuels or Carbon Credits for Hard-to-Abate Transport?
items.synopsisMd:
Hard-to-abate transport sectors face a difficult decarbonization choice: pay for scarce low-carbon fuel alternatives, rely on carbon credits, or use a combination of both. Aviation is the clearest test case, with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandates, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (Corsia) and corporate Scope 3 pressure already reshaping airline choices. But the same questions are emerging across other transport sectors as fuel users evaluate biofuels, e-fuels and other lower-carbon fuels. 
 
Are mandates creating real markets for sustainable fuels, or exposing a gap between policy ambition and available supply? Can SAF and e-fuels become investable at scale, or will constraints related to feedstock, hydrogen, carbon sourcing and infrastructure limit growth? What will determine the balance between fuel-based reductions and carbon market compliance?

items.name: "Made in Europe" Put to the Test: What Should Europe Fight to Keep?
items.synopsisMd: The European Union wants to build up its clean-tech manufacturing base, but recent bankruptcies in batteries, solar and other emerging sectors have exposed just how difficult it is to compete globally. At the same time, Europe remains home to world-leading industrial champions in sectors such as wind turbines, gas turbines and power equipment. What lessons can policymakers draw from these enduring success stories? How important is it to preserve local industrial know-how, engineering expertise and supply chains as the energy transition accelerates? As Brussels considers local-content rules, investment screening, tariffs and other industrial policy tools, where should Europe double down on its competitive advantages - and where should it lean on global supply chains? Which technologies are truly strategic, and what does a successful industrial strategy look like beyond simply making everything at home?

items.name: Stocktake: What the Burnham Era Spells for Britain's Energy Transition Supply Chains
items.subtitle: Roundtable hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd:
Three big questions loom over manufacturers as the Burnham government shapes its industrial agenda. Will Britain lean on open trade to keep renewables deployment cheap, or adopt Brussels’ increasingly tough approach to Chinese clean-tech imports? Can it keep UK-built EV exports tariff-free as UK-EU rules of origin tighten? And what would linking the UK and EU carbon markets spell for heavy industry, from carbon costs and CBAM exposure to export competitiveness? Much depends on where the government is willing to compromise, and whether Burnham has the political capital to follow through. 

This is an invite-only event. If you are interested in attending please reach out to Matthew Hales ([mhales5@bloomberg.net](mhales5@bloomberg.net)).

items.name: Energy Supply Banking Ratios: Latest Results and Evolving Bank Practice
items.subtitle: Roundtable hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd:
BNEF’s forthcoming update will examine whether bank financing is shifting toward low-carbon energy supply relative to fossil fuels, and how the picture changes under a new capex-based methodology. This session will share the results, compare how banks are developing and applying their own ratios, and discuss where the ratio can inform client engagement, sector strategy and business development. 

*This is an invite-only event. If you are interested in attending please reach out to Alex Rushing ([arushing4@bloomberg.net](arushing4@bloomberg.net)).*

items.name: Building Resilient Energy Storage: From Supply Chain to Bottom Line
items.subtitle: Roundtable hosted by Sunwoda
items.synopsisMd:
The energy storage sector is being reshaped by forces well beyond the battery cell. Trade barriers and domestic manufacturing requirements in the US and European Union are disrupting established supply chains, while the EU Batteries Regulation is introducing a new layer of compliance cost and complexity. At the same time, developers and investors are under growing pressure to translate capital spending into long-term returns. This roundtable will bring together industry leaders to discuss how geopolitics, regulation and project economics are together redefining what it takes to build and operate a competitive BESS business. 

*This is an invite-only event. If you are interested in attending, please reach out to Yiran Bian ([ybian35@bloomberg.net](ybian35@bloomberg.net)). *

items.name: Financing Zero-Emission Road Freight at Scale
items.subtitle: Roundtable hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd:
Freight sits at the heart of the global economy, but it also represents one of the toughest decarbonization challenges. Sales of zero-emission trucks are rising as more operations become economically competitive with diesel. As the market moves beyond early adoption, scaling deployment now depends less on technology and more on financing, infrastructure and business models. 

Investor interest is growing. But uncertainty over residual values, asset utilization and infrastructure economics continues to raise the cost of capital, restricting lending. 

This closed-doors roundtable will bring together senior leaders from finance, fleet operations, infrastructure, manufacturing and policy. They will examine the financing models, investment risks and commercial partnerships needed to accelerate deployment at scale. 
 
*This is an invite-only event. If you are interested in attending, please reach out to Niko Soulopoulos ([nsoulopoulos @bloomberg.net](nsoulopoulos @bloomberg.net)). *

items.name: The Geopolitics of Supply: Oil, Gas and a Fragmenting Global Market
items.subtitle: Senior Executive Roundtable hosted by BloombergNEF
items.synopsisMd:
Geopolitical risk is becoming a core market fundamental for oil and gas. From sanctions, tariffs and export controls to instability in Venezuela and the Middle East and intensifying competition with China, political decisions are increasingly determining where hydrocarbons are produced, how they are transported, and who can buy them at what price.

This senior executive roundtable will examine how geopolitical flashpoints are reshaping oil, gas and LNG markets. Participants will consider the resilience of key producing regions and shipping routes, as well as the implications of sanctions enforcement, shifting trade relationships and infrastructure constraints.

More broadly, the discussion will focus on how business leaders can distinguish short-term market noise from structural change, identify vulnerabilities across their portfolios and supply chains, and prepare for a more fragmented and volatile global energy system.

This is an invite-only event. If you are interested in attending please reach out to Polina Andreeva ([pandreeva2@bloomberg.net](mailto:pandreeva2@bloomberg.net)).
